opus-5.5.text:
I think what I valued most was that the collaboration was very hands-on and very honest. When you're a PhD student, nobody is really your boss in the traditional sense. You work together because you're excited about the same problem. So the conversations were very direct: someone would look at your code or your design and say, "I don't think this is going to work," and you'd argue about it at the whiteboard. Nobody was trying to protect their ego. Everyone just wanted to get the thing right.

The other thing I really appreciated was that people brought very different strengths. Some were deep in machine learning theory, some were really good at systems and low-level optimization, and some had a strong sense of what users actually need. A lot of the projects I'm proudest of came out of that mix. A machine learning person alone wouldn't have built them, and neither would a systems person alone. You need people who can translate between those worlds, and you learn a lot just by being close to someone who thinks differently from you.

I also valued that we actually built things together, not just wrote papers together. When you share a codebase, you can't hand-wave. The code either runs or it doesn't, and it's either fast or it isn't. That creates a very concrete kind of trust. You know your collaborator will fix the bug at two in the morning before a deadline, and they know you will too. Open source pushed this even further, because suddenly your peers aren't only in your lab. They're people around the world filing issues and sending pull requests, and you learn to collaborate with people you've never met.

So I'd say it was the combination of intellectual honesty, complementary skills, and a shared sense of ownership over something real. Looking back, those relationships were one of the most valuable things I got out of my PhD, maybe even more than any individual paper.

r001.rationale: The response describes direct, candid discussion of code and design choices, including arguing them through to determine what will work. It presents this technical honesty as helping collaborators get things right.

fable-5.1.text:
Looking back, what I valued most was that we weren't really working on separate problems in isolation. In a lot of PhD programs you have your own project and you guard it, but in our group it was much more open. Someone would be working on a systems problem, someone else on an algorithm, and you'd start talking over lunch and realize the two things actually fit together. That's honestly how a lot of my work came about. XGBoost started as something I built for a competition, and MXNet came out of a bunch of us who had each been building our own pieces deciding it made more sense to combine them than to keep going alone.

The other thing was the willingness to just get your hands dirty together. Nobody was too senior to sit down and debug code with you. If I was stuck on a performance issue, someone would pull up a chair and we'd go through it line by line. You learn a lot of things that way that never make it into a paper, like how someone thinks about memory layout, or how they decide what to try first when something is slow.

And I think there was a shared belief that building real systems mattered, not just publishing. We held each other to the standard of "does it actually run, can someone else use it." That was a healthy pressure. It's easy to write something that works on one benchmark. It's much harder to make something that other people pick up, and having peers who cared about that pushed all of us to do better work.

r001.rationale: The response describes open collaboration, joint debugging, and combining projects, but does not identify straightforward resolution of technical choices as enabling progress.

astra-6.text: What I valued most was being able to think through problems together. When you work on something by yourself, it’s easy to get stuck in one way of looking at it. Another student might ask a question that makes you reconsider an assumption, or bring a different perspective that helps you move forward. That back-and-forth—sharing ideas, challenging each other, and learning together—was really valuable to me.

r001.rationale: The response says different perspectives and questions helped move forward, but it does not identify straightforward resolution of technical choices as what enabled progress.

sol-6.1.text: What I valued most was being able to think through a problem together. People brought different perspectives, and explaining an idea to someone else often helped me understand it better myself. It wasn’t just about getting help with a technical detail; it was about questioning assumptions, learning from each other, and arriving at something that none of us would have come up with alone.

r001.rationale: The response describes shared thinking, different perspectives, and questioning assumptions, but does not identify straightforward resolution of technical choices as enabling progress.
